title: Third-method insurance: find a family whose success is uncorrelated with both (★) and b=1
connection: Holowinsky–Soundararajan needed exactly two complementary methods. ES data show (★) ∪ b=1 never fail together ≤ 10⁸, but a proof-grade argument may need a third family whose success correlates with neither (e.g. ES₅, Type I lines, small windows). Measure correlations of success indicators among 6–8 families.
why: Identifies the minimal robust family set for a complementary-methods proof.
first_step: Compute the correlation matrix of family success indicators (and of their counts) over primes ≤ 10⁸ in Mordell-hard classes.
refs: arXiv:0809.1636 (Holowinsky-Soundararajan, Mass equidistribution for Hecke eigenforms)

title: Finite base + closure: what finite verification would an ES closure theorem need?
connection: Graham's 77-theorem needed a finite check (78–333) plus closure maps. If any closure/transfer system for ES certificates were found (see closure items), compute the minimal 'base' of verified instances it needs; ES is verified to 10¹⁸, so any closure system with base ≤ 10¹⁸ would finish.
why: Turns closure-map searches into a concrete success criterion.
first_step: For each candidate closure map found by search, compute the set of primes it reaches from primes ≤ 10⁶ and check whether its complement thins out.
refs: Graham, A theorem on partitions, J. Austral. Math. Soc. 3 (1963) 435-441 (77-theorem); see also Graham, Pacific J. Math. 10 (1960) 1221-1224 / OEIS A051882 (subagent dating conflict: check)

title: Limit objects of normalised divisor-class data as p → ∞ (Sendov's limiting measures)
connection: Tao's Sendov proof studies limiting zero distributions. For ES, attach to p the empirical measure of (log d / log N, class of d mod 4C) over levels C ≤ K and divisors d of 4Cp + 1; study its limit as p → ∞ (should be a product of uniform measures) and the rate; a counterexample sequence would converge to a measure avoiding a fixed 'certificate region'.
why: Gives a concrete limit object for compactness arguments.
first_step: Compute these empirical measures for p ~ 10⁶, 10⁸, 10¹⁰ and measure distance to the product-uniform model.
refs: arXiv:2012.04125 (Tao, Sendov's conjecture for sufficiently high degree polynomials)

title: Nagao amalgam: SL₂(F_q[T]) is not finitely generated — the words form of ES changes shape
connection: ES ⇔ certain short SL₂(Z) words; SL₂(F_q[T]) is an amalgam (Nagao) of GL₂(F_q)-type and Borel pieces and is not finitely generated, so word length is replaced by degree.
why: If the FF words problem is trivial via the Borel piece, it shows that ES words over Z draw their difficulty from SL₂(Z)'s finite generation.
first_step: Translate the SL₂ word form of ES to SL₂(F_q[T]) and check whether Borel elements produce solutions for all P.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Engel and Pierce expansions: ES as a length-3 Engel-type representation
connection: Chain solutions (x | y | z) are Engel-like (1/x(1 + 1/a(1 + 1/b))). Engel/Pierce expansions of 4/n are deterministic; their lengths give a dynamical invariant.
why: If a variant of Engel expansion of 4/n always has length ≤ 3 after a single 'reset', ES follows; computing it is cheap.
first_step: Compute the Engel expansion length of 4/p for p ≤ 10^5; correlate with chain-world failures (38 below 4000).
refs: scripts/z52b_analogues_constraints.py (p ≡ 1 mod 4, p < 4000, all solutions enumerated)

title: Hirzebruch–Jung continued fractions and cyclic quotient singularities ↔ ES₅
connection: ES₅ (continued-fraction length ≤ 3) can be read as a statement about cyclic quotient singularities 1/p(1, q) whose HJ continued fraction (resolution graph) has a specific short shape.
why: Toric geometry gives operations (blow-ups, Wahl/T-singularities) acting on continued fractions; ES might be equivalent to the existence of a short resolution chain.
first_step: Translate λ(p) ≤ 3 into an HJ-continued-fraction condition on some q mod p and check against bsA_toric_ksb_wahl.md.

title: Apollonian/Descartes: curvatures with reciprocal relations
connection: Descartes' theorem relates curvatures quadratically; Apollonian packings carry orbit structure (thin groups) with local–global principles (Bourgain–Kontorovich density one; failures found by Haag–Kertzer–Rickards–Stange). ES's reciprocal-sum structure is linear in curvatures 1/x.
why: Apollonian local–global failure via reciprocity (quadratic/quartic obstructions) is the closest known analogue of T1: an orbit problem where a reciprocity obstruction removes a density-zero but infinite set.
first_step: Read Haag–Kertzer–Rickards–Stange (local-global failures in Apollonian packings) and compare their reciprocity obstruction with T1 at odd squares.

title: Ford circles / Farey: 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/n as a tangency/curvature condition
connection: Farey neighbours and Ford circles encode 1/(qq') differences; three unit fractions summing to 4/n can be read as a chain of Farey steps. The repo's Farey/forest forms are instances.
why: Already explored (forests); keep as a pointer to the Farey world where SL₂(Z) acts.
first_step: Pointer only; check BRAINSTORM/farey_ford_cf.md.

title: Cluster algebras / friezes: unit fractions from Conway–Coxeter friezes
connection: Friezes encode continued fractions and SL₂ words; ES₅/SL₂-word forms suggest a frieze pattern of width ≤ 3 that produces 4/p. The repo has FRIEZE_ES.
why: Pointer: cluster mutation is a natural 'transport' between solutions.
first_step: Check whether the ES₅ length-3 words correspond to 3×(width) frieze patterns with entries tied to p, per FRIEZE_ES.md.
alt_first_steps: [analogues-0181] Pointer only; read FRIEZE_ES.md for status.
[free_opus-0075] Search for a frieze pattern of width ≤ 3 whose quiddity contains p-tied entries and whose positivity is ES₅.
[signature-0332] Check whether ES’s cubic surface can be embedded as a rank-two cluster recurrence with a positivity invariant; begin with its trilinear identity.
refs: Lee–Schiffler, Positivity for cluster algebras, Ann. Math. 182 (2015), arXiv:1306.2415

title: q-deformed rationals (Morier-Genoud–Ovsienko) and the continued-fraction form ES₅
connection: q-deformed rationals [a/b]_q are defined via continued fractions; ES₅ characterizes ES via continued-fraction length. A q-ES₅ statement could be stated for [4/p]_q and tested for positivity of coefficients.
why: q-rationals have total positivity and Jones-polynomial interpretations; a positivity statement for q-ES₅ might be provable and specialize at q = 1.
first_step: Check whether Morier-Genoud–Ovsienko 'q-deformed rationals and q-continued fractions' (Forum Math. Sigma 2020) defines sums; test [4/p]_q against sums of three q-unit fractions.

title: Dynamical world: Farey/Gauss map orbits of 4/p and 'three-step returns'
connection: ES₅ (length ≤ 3) asks for short orbits of a map on rationals. In the dynamical world, random rationals have orbit lengths ~ log p; ES needs a 'short-cut' orbit of length 3 for one of many starting points tied to p.
why: Dynamical large-deviation results (orbit lengths of rationals) give probability of short orbits; summing over available starting points recovers the log² heuristic.
first_step: Check repo's z31_dynamics_ergodic.md; compute the distribution of minimal ES₅ lengths over starting points for p ≤ 10^4.

title: McMullen's uniformly diophantine numbers in a fixed quadratic field ↔ periodic HJ data
connection: McMullen showed every real quadratic field contains infinitely many periodic continued fractions with bounded partial quotients. ES words relate to quadratic data via γ_w (trace A + A*). A quadratic-field-uniform statement is a model for 'certificates in every class'.
why: It is one of the rare pointwise CF theorems proved by a non-expansion argument (closed geodesics, Hecke-type operators).
first_step: Read McMullen 'Uniformly Diophantine numbers in a fixed real quadratic field' (Compositio 2009) and check whether its geodesic-construction trick could prescribe a trace/level relation like ES's.
refs: McMullen, Uniformly Diophantine numbers in a fixed real quadratic field (Compos. Math. 2009)

title: Feature: thin-orbit expansion (SL₂ spectral gap)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'thin-orbit expansion (SL₂ spectral gap)'. ES LACKS: ES₅ is a fixed-length-3 word problem, no growing word length. To supply it one could: allow longer words with a constraint that collapses them to length 3 (as Zaremba's alphabet size tunes counts); check if a 'length-collapsing' identity exists
why: Zaremba / Apollonian density-one results need orbits whose size grows as a power.
first_step: None new (ZAREMBA_TRANSFER.md).

title: Between: Hensley alphabet at critical dimension δ_A = 1/2
connection: Thin-orbit CF problems at exactly the critical exponent have count ≍ polylog — the closest SL₂ analogue of ES₅.
why: Results (or failures) at δ = 1/2 would tell whether polylog-count thin-orbit statements can be pointwise.
first_step: Search literature for 'critical dimension 1/2 Zaremba' and compute denominators covered for an alphabet tuned to δ ≈ 1/2.

title: Transfer: Zagier-style involution on I3 words p = tuv − u − v
connection: The I3 reformulation gives a finite set of (t,u,v); look for an involution composed of 'flip' moves (u ↔ v, and a windmill-type move) with a unique fixed point.
why: Windmill involutions prove two squares for p ≡ 1 mod 4 using only a finite set and parity; ES has finite certificate sets too.
first_step: Compute #{(t,u,v): tuv − u − v = p, t,u,v ≥ 1 with coordinate in 4ℤ ∪ (8ℤ − p)} mod 2 for p ≡ 1 mod 24 ≤ 10^5.

title: Transfer: Ergodic 'measure rigidity' for exceptional primes
connection: EKL show Littlewood exceptions have dimension 0 via measure rigidity of diagonal flows; ES exceptions (if any) might correspond to divergent/escaping orbits in some homogeneous space.
why: If ES certificates correspond to orbit intersections in a homogeneous space, rigidity could restrict exceptional sets.
first_step: Look for a homogeneous dynamics model: e.g. the CF/SL₂ words of ES₅ as visits of a geodesic to a cusp region.

title: Expander-free 'thin' structure: ES₅ words as length-3 paths in the Farey graph
connection: ES₅ ⟺ λ(p) ≤ 3: a short path in the Farey/Stern–Brocot graph between specific vertices. Graph distance ≤ 3 problems in growing graphs with no expansion argument.
why: Diameter/short-path existence results in arithmetic graphs (e.g. Cayley graphs of SL₂(ℤ/p)) are proved by expansion only at log diameter, not fixed length.
first_step: See BRAINSTORM/bsA_farey_graph_metric.md.

title: Fixed-length words in SL₂(ℤ): Waring problem for SL₂ / word maps
connection: Every element of SL₂(ℤ/p) is a product of ≤ 3 (or bounded) elements of a given type (Waring for word maps; Larsen–Shalev). ES₅ is a fixed-length word condition in SL₂(ℤ) with integrality.
why: Bounded-width results in finite groups are proved by character theory (Frobenius formula) — a 'thick' count over the group — but ES needs integral lifts.
first_step: Check whether the ES₅ word count over SL₂(ℤ/N) is given by a Frobenius character formula and whether lifting to ℤ is the only gap.

title: Bounded generation of SL₂(ℤ[1/p]) / elementary matrices (Carter–Keller, Vsemirnov)
connection: Bounded generation results (every matrix a product of ≤ N elementary matrices) are pointwise for every element, proved by arithmetic (Dirichlet's theorem) — closest to 'fixed-length word exists for every target'.
why: ES₅ is an existence of a fixed-length word; bounded generation proofs use primes in APs to steer entries.
first_step: Read Vsemirnov / Morgan–Rapinchuk–Sury on bounded generation of SL₂(ℤ[1/p]) and compare the word shape with ES₅'s.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: t=1 and t=2 word counts are τ(n+1) and τ(2n+1) (OEIS A000005, A099774)
connection: The t=1 slice of tuv−u−v=n is (u−1)(v−1)=n+1 → τ(n+1); the t=2 slice is (2u−1)(2v−1)=2n+1 → τ(2n+1) (OEIS confirmed).
why: Sanity anchor for the word sieve, and a reminder that each t-slice is a divisor function of tn+1 restricted to −1 mod t — the 'tied-modulus divisor event'.
first_step: None (anchor); use as unit tests.

title: U(p) vs CF period of √p (ρ = −0.27)
connection: Longer CF period of √p (larger regulator) ⇒ fewer ES solutions.
why: ES has continued-fraction reformulations (ES₅, λ(p) ≤ 3); the CF of √p is a different object, but the correlation goes through L(1,χ_p) = 2hR/√p.
first_step: Partial correlation of U with CF period controlling for L(1,χ_p); if ≈ 0, the CF of √p carries nothing extra.

title: Continued fraction of 4/p and its partial quotients vs U(p)
connection: 4/p has a short CF; ES₅ ⟺ λ(p) ≤ 3 is about CF lengths of p/A for certain A. Correlate U(p) with the CF length/max partial quotient of p/A over small A.
why: Bridges the CF formulation (Zaremba-type, ZAREMBA_TRANSFER.md) to the count; a strong correlation would suggest Zaremba/Bourgain–Kontorovich density tools apply.
first_step: For each p compute #{A < p : CF length of p/A ≤ 3} (the five-slice count) and Spearman with U(p).

title: Hirzebruch–Jung length fingerprint of hard primes
connection: λ(p) (minimal HJ/CF length certificate) for hard primes vs random: are hard primes the ones with λ(p) = 3 exactly (no length-2 certificates)?
why: λ(p) is a discrete hardness grade; its distribution conditional on χ_p would connect CF dynamics with the Euler-product count law.
first_step: Compute λ(p) for p ≤ 10⁵ (existing scripts? check scripts/*hj*) and cross-tabulate with U(p)/log² quantiles.

title: 105 is the unique non-square n ≡ 1 (4) ≤ 3·10⁶ killing all three word families
connection: R(105) = Uv(105) = I3(105) = 0 and ESC(105) = 0; every other non-square n ≡ 1 (4) has at least two families alive.
why: 105 = 3·5·7 is 'locally square' modulo 8 and small primes? (105 ≡ 1 mod 8, 105 ≡ 0 mod 3,5,7) — its divisibility by 3,5,7 kills shifts; a structural characterisation would explain uniqueness.
first_step: Check whether n = 3·5·7·m² or other 'n ≡ 0 mod 105' families have systematically few words.

title: Moving the first denominator
connection: Connect changes x→x+1 with changes in the residual factor-pair problem, treating consecutive x as coupled rather than independent trials.
why: Neighboring residual numerators differ by four, so their divisor searches share arithmetic structure.
first_step: Tabulate success transitions between neighboring x for 100 primes.

title: Weighted mediants
connection: Compare residual fractions from neighboring x with Farey mediants, looking for intervals where a two-term decomposition persists.
why: Farey adjacency controls numerator-denominator determinants exactly.
first_step: Compute Farey neighbors of residual fractions for the first 50 difficult primes.

title: Cluster-style mutations
connection: Search for involutions on auxiliary ES parametrizations analogous to replacing one root of a quadratic while fixing other variables.
why: An exact positive integral mutation could propagate certificates across a connected graph.
first_step: For three existing elementary parametrizations, solve for each coordinate and test whether another integral branch exists.

title: Continued-fraction surgery
connection: Study local replacements in continued fractions that change a certificate's congruence data without making its length too large.
why: Equivalent rational expansions can trade coefficient signs, sizes, and parity.
first_step: Enumerate short continued-fraction identities and label which preserve positivity and desired coefficient classes.

title: Continuants modulo powers of two
connection: Analyze short continuant recurrences modulo 8,16,32 and compare reachable states with the admissible coordinate classes.
why: Finite parity information may guide an otherwise unbounded integer construction.
first_step: Build the exact transition graph for continuants modulo 16 with coefficient residues as labels.

title: Stern–Brocot ancestry
connection: Attach each residual rational to its Stern–Brocot path and look for common terminal patterns among successful splits.
why: Path suffixes may encode useful divisibility conditions more compactly than numerator-denominator pairs.
first_step: Record path suffixes of length at most eight for successful and unsuccessful bounded residual searches.

title: Euclidean quotient parity
connection: Track parity of Euclidean quotients together with remainder size when processing p and an auxiliary parameter.
why: Parity-decorated Euclidean descent could interact with the required classes modulo four.
first_step: Compute quotient-parity strings for certificates found by a fixed divisor search and compare with controls.

title: Semigroup holes
connection: Treat attainable certificate parameters under positive identity composition as an affine semigroup and inspect its holes.
why: Eventual saturation is a meaningful possibility even when small exceptions persist.
first_step: Generate the semigroup from a small set of verified composition moves and compute missing points in a bounded region.

title: Regular languages of valid matrix words
connection: Describe congruence-admissible matrix words by a finite automaton and distinguish this from their unbounded integer values.
why: Congruence admissibility is genuinely finite-state, providing a rigorous symbolic skeleton.
first_step: Build an automaton for elementary matrices modulo 8 with accepting states matching one required coordinate condition.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Markov bases for certificate fibers
connection: Seek finite move sets connecting all nonnegative solutions of a fixed linearized parameter constraint.
why: Connectivity of the linear fiber could reduce enumeration before nonlinear conditions are imposed.
first_step: Compute a kernel basis for a toy exponent-allocation matrix and test which moves preserve positivity.

title: Lax-pair discovery as an algebraic search
connection: Ask whether a certificate-preserving transformation admits a matrix conjugation description with invariant characteristic polynomial.
why: A Lax representation would expose conserved quantities, not by itself guarantee positive integer orbits.
first_step: For one verified rational map, search two-by-two matrix entries of low degree satisfying the conjugation equation.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Symplectic coordinates for matrix words
connection: Use the area-preserving action of SL₂ on pairs of coordinates to track certificate-related invariants.
why: An invariant determinant can constrain possible moves more cleanly than expanded polynomials.
first_step: Choose two column vectors from a short word and compute which parameter changes preserve their determinant and residue labels.

title: Modular geodesic coding
connection: Compare continued-fraction certificate words with symbolic codes of geodesic segments on the modular surface.
why: Geometric coding may organize word length and cusp excursions, while the ES condition remains arithmetic.
first_step: Translate several short certificate words into matrices and compute their fixed points and trace types.

title: Horocycle sampling of congruence states
connection: Study elementary unipotent matrix orbits modulo small integers and their integer-height growth.
why: These are explicit orbits that could generate systematic candidate families.
first_step: Enumerate products of two unipotent flows modulo 16 and track the least integer height realizing each target state.

title: Skew products coupling size and residue
connection: Track a real size coordinate together with a finite residue state under a certificate-related recurrence.
why: This separates growth from arithmetic admissibility while keeping their interaction explicit.
first_step: Build the skew-product map for a short Euclidean or matrix recurrence and plot admissible returns.

title: Interval-exchange selectors
connection: Use interval maps associated with rational approximation to partition parameter choices into symbolic regimes.
why: A finite partition might yield a small list of exact denominator formulas on each regime.
first_step: Compute return itineraries for a simple interval map and test whether an exact residual formula is constant in symbolic type.

title: Periodic-orbit certificate families
connection: Search for parameter recurrences with periodic residue states and nonperiodic integer growth.
why: A periodic modular pattern can preserve admissibility along an infinite arithmetic orbit.
first_step: For one exact recurrence, enumerate cycles modulo 8 and verify which lifted initial points remain positive integers.

title: Return-time distributions
connection: Measure first visits to admissible residue states in deterministic certificate-generating dynamics.
why: Return-time tails are directly connected to the cost of the resulting search procedure.
first_step: For several initial states, record first-hit times and compare them with orbit component sizes.

title: Arithmetic cocycles
connection: Record a multiplicative scale factor and a congruence correction along each matrix or continued-fraction move.
why: The cocycle may reveal telescoping products that enforce integrality after a whole word.
first_step: Compute the scale cocycle for three verified moves and search short loops with unit total correction.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Invariant discovery with counterexamples
connection: Search low-degree expressions constant under verified certificate transformations, rejecting candidates on fresh exact examples.
why: A discovered invariant can organize orbit structure and explain why some moves fail to connect families.
first_step: Solve linear equations for quadratic invariants of one transformation and check survivors symbolically.

title: Engel expansions as intermediate representations
connection: Compare multiplicative-denominator Engel expansions of 4/p with ordinary unit-fraction decompositions and possible regroupings.
why: Nested denominator structure may make some exact merges easier to describe.
first_step: Compute short Engel expansions for small primes and test adjacent-term merges into a single unit fraction.

title: Lüroth-style digit systems
connection: Check whether a rational expansion with consecutive-product denominators can be converted into a useful three-term ES ansatz.
why: The digit system offers a different exact decomposition grammar, not an automatic short representation.
first_step: Verify the precise Lüroth expansion formula and test finite rational examples for algebraically valid regroupings.

title: Ostrowski numeration of parameter choices
connection: Use continued-fraction-based numeration to encode auxiliary integers relative to p and a chosen modulus.
why: The digits may align with Euclidean recurrences and make congruence repair more local.
first_step: For one rational rotation, write several successful auxiliary values in Ostrowski coordinates and compare their digit patterns.

title: Polynomial continued fractions
connection: Compare short continued fractions over Fq[T] with the integer word formulations, retaining coefficient degree and unit information.
why: The Euclidean algorithm survives, but ordering and parity constraints change substantially.
first_step: Compute length-three expansions over F5[T] and identify which coefficient conditions correspond to the integer formulation.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Indefinite quadratic-form orbits
connection: Study indefinite quadratic slices using reduction and automorphisms rather than finite ellipsoid enumeration.
why: Infinite orbits may generate recurrent witnesses, with positivity handled along the orbit.
first_step: For one binary indefinite form arising from a slice, compute a fundamental automorphism and its residues modulo 8.

title: Frenkel–Kontorova / devil's staircase of the 'best C' function
connection: C_min(p) (smallest C with a winning divisor) as a function of p may show a staircase structure with plateaus at values tied to Mordell classes; devil's staircases arise from mode-locking in circle maps.
why: Mode-locking = rational rotation numbers = continued fractions, which is already an ES reformulation (ES₅).
first_step: Plot C_min(p) against p for p ≡ 1 mod 24 up to 10⁷; look for plateau structure and its relation to p mod 840.

title: Error-correcting codes: solution sets as codewords, and ES as 'minimum distance ≥ 1 from the zero word'
connection: Define for each p the binary vector v_p ∈ {0,1}^K with v_p[C] = 1 if C wins. ES(p) for C ≤ K ⟺ v_p ≠ 0. The set {v_p} is a 'code'; its minimum weight (over p) and its dual structure may reveal linear constraints among the C's.
why: Linear constraints among win-events (over F₂) would be exactly the parity invariants that could force a win.
first_step: Compute v_p for K = 64 and p ≤ 10⁶; compute the F₂-rank of the matrix and look for low-weight dual codewords (parity checks).

title: Egyptian fraction 'Engel expansion' and 'Pierce expansion' of 4/p: alternative canonical expansions with ≤ 3 terms?
connection: Engel expansion writes x = 1/a₁ + 1/(a₁a₂) + 1/(a₁a₂a₃) + …; Pierce alternates signs. For 4/p, the Engel expansion's length and the possibility of truncation/modification to 3 unit fractions is an unexplored canonical form.
why: Canonical expansions with algebraic structure (Engel: a_{k+1} determined by a_k) might make 'length 3' a tractable condition like ES₅'s CF length.
first_step: Compute Engel expansions of 4/p for p ≤ 10⁴; count lengths; check whether a length-3 Engel expansion exists for all p (unlikely) or whether the Engel denominators relate to Type I/II parameters.

title: Stern–Brocot / Farey neighbours: 4/p's Farey parents and the two-term splitting 4/p = 1/x + (4x−p)/(px)
connection: Farey neighbours a/b, c/d with bc − ad = 1 give 1/(bd) = c/d − a/b; a unit-fraction-friendly structure. Writing 4/p as a sum of unit fractions via Farey-neighbour chains of length 3.
why: The repo has Farey items (bsA_farey_*); the free-lane twist: is there a 'Farey path' interpretation where ES = path of length 3 in the Farey graph from 4/p to 0 with unit-fraction steps? That's close to the CF/ES₅ form; worth making explicit.
first_step: git grep -il farey BRAINSTORM | head; then compute for p ≤ 1000 the Farey-graph distance from 4/p to 0 under 'subtract a unit fraction' moves.

title: Music/tilings: 4/p as a rhythm — Euclidean rhythms and unit-fraction tilings of the circle
connection: Tiling a circle of circumference 4 by three arcs of lengths p/x, p/y, p/z... i.e. 4 = p/x + p/y + p/z — a tiling of [0,4] by rational lengths with a common 'p' numerator. Euclidean rhythms (Toussaint) relate to Bjorklund's algorithm = Euclid's algorithm = continued fractions.
why: Recreational lens that lands on continued fractions again; perhaps a rhythmic 'evenness' measure corresponds to CF length ≤ 3.
first_step: Just note the reformulation; compute whether the Bjorklund rhythm E(4, p) decomposes into 3 'regular' sub-rhythms iff ES solution exists with specific structure — 15 minutes.
refs: Toussaint, 'The Euclidean algorithm generates traditional musical rhythms' (2005)

title: Semigroup orbit reformulation: Type II certificates as products of two 'elementary' matrices in a congruence semigroup
connection: 4Cp + 1 = (4Cu − 1)(4Cv − 1). Consider matrices M_C(u) = [[4Cu − 1, ?],[?, ?]] in SL₂? E.g. the matrix [[4Cu−1, −u],[−4C·?..]] — find a representation where the product M_C(u)·M_C(v) has p as an entry. Try: A_u = [[1, u],[0, 1]]·[[1, 0],[−4C, 1]]·... Standard: the continued fraction [0; 4C, u, ...]? Let's just make it an experiment.
why: If Type II certificates are entries of products in a 2-generator semigroup (parametrised by C), then 'p appears as an entry' is a thin-orbit problem with the level 4C — same shape as Zaremba (where the semigroup is fixed and q is the entry). The novelty: the semigroup depends on C, but p must appear for SOME C — a union over C of thin orbits.
first_step: Find matrices in SL₂(ℤ) whose (1,1)-entry of a length-2 product is (4Cu−1)(4Cv−1) − 1)/(4C) = p for integers u,v (e.g. [[4Cu−1, u],[4C·?, ?]] with det 1 forces entries); if found, compare with the ES₅ word of length 3.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Numeration systems: Ostrowski numeration (based on the CF of a fixed irrational) and Zeckendorf — is there a numeration system in which 'n has an ES certificate' is a digit condition?
connection: Automatic-sequence-style question in a non-standard numeration: some sets defined by CF data (e.g. Beatty sequences) are recognisable in Ostrowski numeration (Hieronymi–Terry). ES₅ is a CF condition on a p-tied rational; maybe recognisable in a suitable numeration, making Walnut-style decision procedures applicable to sub-statements.
why: Long shot; but Ostrowski-automatic sets are a modern decidable class that includes CF-defined sets.
first_step: Read Hieronymi–Terry 'Ostrowski numeration systems, addition, and finite automata'; check if 'CF length of r(p) ≤ 3' can be phrased for p in a fixed Ostrowski system.
refs: Hieronymi–Terry, Notre Dame J. Formal Logic 2018

title: Collatz analogy: 'stopping time' of a certificate search as a function of p vs Collatz stopping times — both have log-ish expected values with no pointwise proof; what do Collatz researchers' heuristics (Tao's almost-all result via logarithmic density) suggest for ES?
connection: Tao (2019) proved almost all Collatz orbits attain almost bounded values via a 'logarithmic density + invariant measure' argument; ES has almost-all results via sieve. The Collatz pointwise question remains open for the same 'no reservoir' reason. Structural comparison: Collatz has a dynamical system; ES has none (no orbit) — see the orbit-absence lemma. So ES is 'Collatz without the map'.
why: Comparison sharpens what ES lacks (a map) and what it has (algebra: factorisations); a hybrid (define a map on certificates) is the 'Lyapunov function' item.
first_step: Read Tao's Collatz paper intro for the heuristic model and see if the 'Syracuse random variable' method has an ES analogue (random model of the factorisation of 4Cp+1 as C varies — the Kubilius model item).
refs: Tao, 'Almost all orbits of the Collatz map attain almost bounded values' (Forum Math Pi 2022)

title: Ellenberg–Venkatesh 'local-global for representations of quadratic forms by forms' as pointwise via ergodic theory
connection: EV proved local-global for representations of a quadratic form by another with an auxiliary splitting prime ↔ ES fibre as 'representation of p by a cubic form family'.
why: Precedent for pointwise results via unipotent dynamics; a Ratner-type input on an ES-associated homogeneous space would be new.
first_step: Check whether ES Type II slice (4uBC − u − B = p) is an orbit-counting problem on a homogeneous space SL₂(ℝ)×… (it is affine in C — maybe).

title: Bourgain–Gamburd expansion in SL₂(ℤ/q) for ES₅ words
connection: Bourgain–Gamburd (and Bourgain–Varjú for composite q) prove Cayley graphs of SL₂(ℤ/q) w.r.t. Zariski-dense generators are expanders; ES₅ / SL₂-word forms of ES express solutions as length-3 words in a fixed generating set.
why: Expansion gives equidistribution of long words; ES fixes length 3, so the relevant input is the short-word distribution — a known barrier (B3) recorded rather than judged.
first_step: Compute the image of all length-≤3 ES₅ words mod q in SL₂(ℤ/q) for q ≤ 200 and measure how much of the target coset they cover.
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0089] For q = small modulus, compute the fraction of SL₂(ℤ/q) hit by ES₅ words with entries ≤ p and compare with random.
refs: Bourgain–Gamburd, Uniform expansion bounds for Cayley graphs of SL2(F_p), Ann. Math. 167 (2008)
Bourgain–Varjú, Expansion in SL_d(Z/qZ), q arbitrary, Invent. Math. 188 (2012)

title: Apollonian packings: Ford circles of 4/p and three tangent circles
connection: Descartes curvatures and Egyptian fractions: Ford circles at a/b have curvature 2b² ↔ 4/p = 1/x+1/y+1/z as a curvature relation?
why: Apollonian local-global (with reciprocity obstructions, HKRS) is the closest 'thin orbit' analogue; a literal geometric embedding of ES into a circle packing would let one import RS/HKRS results.
first_step: Search for a circle configuration whose curvatures are (x,y,z,p) related by 1/x+1/y+1/z = 4/p (inversion of Descartes-type relations).

title: Stern–Brocot / Calkin–Wilf tree paths of 4/p
connection: 4/p's position in the Stern–Brocot tree is encoded by its CF ↔ ES₅ continued-fraction length condition.
why: Tree-path combinatorics (run-length encoding) gives a visual/automaton description of when short Egyptian decompositions exist.
first_step: Compute SB paths of 4/p and of (4x−p)/(px) for successful x; look for a pattern in path run-lengths.

title: Geodesic flow on the modular surface and closed geodesics of discriminant tied to p
connection: Closed geodesics correspond to real quadratic forms; ES certificates might correspond to geodesics passing through a cusp neighbourhood.
why: Equidistribution of closed geodesics (Duke) holds for each large discriminant pointwise — a rare pointwise equidistribution theorem.
first_step: Identify a discriminant D(p) and a target set in the unit tangent bundle such that 'some geodesic of discriminant D(p) visits the set' ⟹ ES(p); check if target set size is ≫ D^{-δ}.

title: Kinetic/flow interpretation: Euclid algorithm as a dynamical system and ES as short-orbit condition
connection: Gauss map dynamics on rationals ↔ ES₅ continued fraction length ≤ 3 for a p-tied rational.
why: Hensley/Baladi–Vallée transfer operators give distribution of CF lengths of rationals with denominator p; ES asks for one rational in a family with short length.
first_step: Use Baladi–Vallée style counting: number of a/p with CF length ≤ 3 and partial quotient constraints; compare with ES₅ counts.

title: Ergodic theory of multiplicative semigroups: Furstenberg ×2×3 and certificates as orbit points
connection: Furstenberg's ×2×3 rigidity ↔ the multiplicative semigroup of divisors of p-tied integers acting on (ℤ/4C)^×.
why: Rigidity theorems give pointwise density of orbits (every infinite ×2×3-invariant closed set is everything); a finite analogue (Bourgain–Lindenstrauss–Michel–Venkatesh effective) gives 'orbits of 2,3 in (ℤ/q)^× are dense'.
first_step: Check BLMV/Bourgain effective ×a×b results: does {2^i 3^j mod q} hit −1 for all q with small exponents? Then ask if 4Cp+1-divisors contain a fixed multiplicative structure.

title: Thermodynamic formalism for Egyptian fraction expansions (Engel/Sylvester series dynamics)
connection: Engel expansions and Sylvester series have ergodic theory (Rényi) ↔ 3-term Egyptian representations as short orbits.
why: Known metric theory of Engel/Sylvester digits could supply heuristic densities for 'expansions of length 3'.
first_step: Compute the Engel/Sylvester (greedy) expansion of 4/p and its length distribution over primes; correlate with ES difficulty.

title: Dynamics on the space of lattices: ES certificates as cusp excursions of a p-indexed orbit
connection: Orbits of diagonal flows on SL₃(ℝ)/SL₃(ℤ) visiting the cusp correspond to small vectors ↔ ES certificates are small vectors in p-dependent lattices.
why: Cusp excursions are governed by Diophantine properties; Littlewood-type pointwise statements are hard but some (Einsiedler–Katok–Lindenstrauss) give measure results.
first_step: Write a 3D lattice Λ_p such that a vector in a specified small cone ⟹ certificate; examine whether the a-orbit of Λ_p is known to enter the cusp region.

title: Chaotic dynamics: the 'Egyptian map' T(a/b) = a/b − 1/⌈b/a⌉ and its periodic structure mod p
connection: Iterating the greedy step on all a/p, a ∈ (ℤ/p)^× defines a map on residues ↔ ES asks about orbits of length ≤ 3 from a = 4 through rescaled fractions.
why: Graph structure of this map on F_p (functional graph) could have computable statistics (tree sizes) related to ES.
first_step: Build the functional graph of the greedy-remainder map on fractions with denominator dividing p·k for small k; compute statistics.

title: Hydrodynamic limit of certificate count as p → ∞ along residue classes
connection: Limit shape of the set of successful (log u/log p, log C/log p) ↔ the main-term density.
why: A limit shape theorem (empirical measure of certificates converges) for almost all p is plausibly provable and would describe where certificates live.
first_step: Plot the empirical measure of (log u, log C)/log p for successful pairs over many p; compare with 1/(uC) density prediction.

title: Odd-square neighbours in the ES₅ word form: tuv − u − v = m² has no 'interior' words? T1 in word language
connection: ES₅ word certificates should exhibit T1 at squares ↔ word-level proof of T1 might identify an invariant (like a Jacobi symbol of t,u,v) that is constant on words.
why: An invariant constant on words but nonconstant on primes would be a hidden conservation law; T1 says it takes a forbidden value on squares.
first_step: Compute the Jacobi symbol combinations (t/·), (u/v)… on all ES₅ words for small n; look for a combination that equals 1 on all words of non-square n... (check repo first).

title: Representation theory of SL₂(ℤ/4C): the Type II condition as a matrix coefficient
connection: SL₂ form [[a,p],[c,d]] with congruences ↔ the count is a matrix coefficient of the permutation representation on cosets.
why: Decomposing into irreducibles separates trivial (main term) and nontrivial (fluctuation) parts — the genus/BM split might be the 1-dim characters; higher irreps carry X(n).
first_step: For small c, compute the permutation representation and its character decomposition; identify which irreps carry the T1 cancellation.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Teichmüller / mapping class group dynamics: SL₂(ℤ) words as Dehn twists on a torus
connection: SL₂(ℤ) = mapping class group of the torus; ES₅ words as products of Dehn twists ↔ curves on a torus with intersection numbers tied to p.
why: Geometric reformulation: ES(p) ⟺ some simple closed curves with prescribed intersection numbers exist — curve-complex combinatorics might give existence arguments.
first_step: Translate an ES₅ word [[a,p],[c,d]] into a pair of simple closed curves on the torus with intersection number p; examine the constraint 'c ∈ 4ℕ, a ≡ d ≡ −1 mod c' geometrically.

title: Combinatorics on words: the Christoffel word / Sturmian structure of continued fraction certificates
connection: Christoffel words encode rationals a/b and their CF ↔ ES₅ CF length ≤ 3 words.
why: Word combinatorics (palindromes, standard factorisation of Christoffel words) may produce a combinatorial proof of existence of a short factorisation.
first_step: Compute Christoffel words of 4/p and of certificate rationals; look for standard factorisations corresponding to ES solutions.

title: ES words are generalised Frobenius numbers: tuv − u − v = g_t(u,v), the largest integer with ≤ t−1 representations by ⟨u,v⟩ (CHECKED)
connection: For coprime u,v the largest n with at most t−1 representations n = au + bv (a,b ≥ 0) is tuv − u − v (t = 1: Sylvester's uv − u − v) ↔ I3/ES₅ words p = tuv − u − v, and (★) is t = 4C: p = 4C·uB − u − B.
why: Puts ES (★)/I3 inside the Frobenius problem / numerical-semigroup theory: ES(★) ⟺ p is the 4C-th 'k-Frobenius number' of some 2-generated semigroup ⟨u,B⟩. That field has its own tools (Apéry sets, Popoviciu's formula, Ehrhart theory, denumerants) and literature on which integers occur as (k-)Frobenius numbers. Not found in repo by grep.
first_step: Verified for u,v < 12, t ≤ 4 (scripts/z52b_free_opus_check3.py). Next: search literature for 'k-Frobenius number' / 'generalized Frobenius number two generators' (Beck–Robins; Brown et al., J. Integer Seq. 2010 — check) and for 'which integers are Frobenius numbers'.

title: Apéry sets and the gap structure of ⟨u,B⟩: p as the maximal element of a 'level-(4C−1)' Apéry-type set
connection: Numerical semigroup S = ⟨u,B⟩: the set of n with exactly k representations has a known structure (shifted Apéry sets) ↔ p must be the top element of the k = 4C − 1 layer.
why: Semigroup-theoretic language may let one treat (u,B) as an unknown semigroup and p as a forced invariant — e.g. counting semigroups of given 'k-Frobenius number' (an inverse problem) could have a generating-function solution.
first_step: Compute, for n ≤ 10⁴, the number of pairs (u,B, t) with g_t(u,B) = n, t ≡ 0 mod 4, and compare with R(n); then look for a semigroup-enumeration generating function.

title: Counting numerical semigroups by Frobenius number (Backelin, Kaplan, Zhai) as a template for 'every p is a k-Frobenius number'
connection: The number of numerical semigroups with Frobenius number F grows like c·2^{F/2} (Backelin) ↔ here restricted to embedding dimension 2 (polylog many) with k-Frobenius.
why: The embedding-dimension-2 restriction collapses the count to divisor-type size (as expected); but allowing embedding dimension 3 semigroups (three generators) might correspond to richer ES-type certificates — check if a 3-generator k-Frobenius identity gives ES solutions.
first_step: Compute Frobenius numbers of 3-generated semigroups ⟨a,b,c⟩ in families and check whether some family's g(a,b,c) formula yields ES certificates (e.g. Type I parametrisation).

title: Representation-count symmetry N(n) + N(g_t − n) = t on [0, g_t] (CHECKED): an involution attached to every ES word
connection: For coprime u,v and g_t = tuv − u − v, the denumerant satisfies N(n) + N(g_t − n) = t for all 0 ≤ n ≤ g_t (generalising symmetry of ⟨u,v⟩ at t = 1) ↔ every ES word p = g_t(u,v) carries the involution n ↦ p − n on representation data.
why: An explicit involution attached to each certificate is the raw material for windmill/parity arguments (G1 parity column); here the involution lives on representations of integers below p rather than on certificates — a different thick object (size ≍ p).
first_step: Verified for u,v ≤ 8, t ≤ 4 (scripts/z52b_free_opus_check3.py). Next: look for a global involution on pairs (n, representation) over all (u,v) whose fixed points correspond to certificates of p; test fixed-point parity on p < 10³.

title: ES words are exactly Frobenius numbers of glued semigroups ⟨tu, tv, u+v⟩
connection: Johnson/Brauer–Shockley gluing gives g(⟨tu, tv, u+v⟩) = t·g(u,v) + (t−1)(u+v) = tuv − u − v when gcd(u,v) = gcd(t,u+v) = 1 (checked by brute force on 488 triples, scripts/z52b_signature_frob_check.py). So the (★) line (words p = 4C·u·B − u − B, which implies ES but itself fails at 14 primes ≤ 10¹⁰) ⟺ p is the Frobenius number of a 3-generated numerical semigroup ⟨4Cu, 4CB, u+B⟩; for (★) words gcd(4C, u+B) = gcd(4C, p) = 1 automatically. The other ES word slices (coordinate in 8ℤ − p, or the 4ℤ coordinate not in the t slot) need a different semigroup family.
why: Rosales–García-Sánchez–García-García–Jiménez Madrid proved every positive integer is the Frobenius number of SOME 3-generated semigroup: the (★) slice of ES is a restriction of a solved universality theorem to a structured sub-family (complete intersections glued from a 2-generated piece); finding semigroup families for the other ES slices would give a full semigroup reformulation of ES.
first_step: Read Rosales et al. (Math. Scand. 94 (2004) 5–12): which 3-generator family does their construction use for odd g, and can it be forced into the shape ⟨tu, tv, u+v⟩ with 4 | t?
refs: J. C. Rosales, P. A. García-Sánchez, J. I. García-García, J. M. Jiménez Madrid, Every positive integer is the Frobenius number of a numerical semigroup with three generators, Math. Scand. 94 (2004) 5–12 (https://journals.msp.org/mscand/article/view/792)

title: Symmetric 3-generated semigroups = complete intersections (Herzog): ES as a symmetric-Frobenius representation problem
connection: Herzog: 3-generated symmetric numerical semigroups are complete intersections, i.e. gluings ⟨d·a, d·b, c⟩ with c ∈ ⟨a,b⟩, gcd(d,c) = 1, whose Frobenius numbers are d(ab − a − b) + (d − 1)c. ES words are the slice c = a + b; other c = αa + βb give other trilinear words dab − a(d − (d−1)α) − b(d − (d−1)β).
why: Gives a natural ambient family (all symmetric 3-generated Frobenius numbers = all odd numbers?) containing the ES words; the question 'which (α,β) slices are universal on primes' is a clean ladder of problems, some maybe solved.
first_step: Enumerate, for odd n ≤ 10⁶, which (α,β) ∈ {0,1,2}² slices of d(ab−a−b)+(d−1)(αa+βb) with 4 | d represent n; compare failure sets with U(n)/T1.
refs: unverified: Herzog 1970, Generators and relations of abelian semigroups and semigroup rings (manuscripta math.)

title: Rødseth/Greenberg 3-generator Frobenius algorithm vs. ES₅ continued-fraction length
connection: The Rødseth algorithm computes g(a,b,c) via a negative-continued-fraction (Euclid) expansion of a ratio mod a; for ⟨tu, tv, u+v⟩ that expansion is short. Compare with λ(p) ≤ 3 (F17).
why: If the Rødseth expansion of the glued semigroup is exactly the length-3 negative CF of the ES₅ form, the semigroup literature (Kannan, Ramírez Alfonsín) becomes a dictionary for ES₅.
first_step: Run Rødseth's algorithm symbolically on ⟨tu, tv, u+v⟩ and record the CF; check against the BOARD2_SLATE ES₅ slice definitions.
refs: unverified: Rødseth 1978, On a linear diophantine problem of Frobenius (J. reine angew. Math.)

title: Genus/Sylvester count of the ES semigroup as a second invariant attached to each witness
connection: Each ES witness (t,u,v) gives a symmetric semigroup S with genus (gaps) (g+1)/2 = (p+1)/2 and an Apéry set of size min generator; these invariants are fixed by p, so ES asks for a semigroup with prescribed Frobenius number and prescribed shape.
why: Counting numerical semigroups by genus is a mature field (Kaplan, Zhai's Fibonacci-like growth); ES asks for one member of a structured subclass among ~φ^g semigroups of genus g — a sparse-subfamily existence question.
first_step: Check OEIS/semigroup tables (e.g. GAP package numericalsgps) for counts of complete-intersection semigroups with given Frobenius number.
refs: unverified: Zhai 2013, Fibonacci-like growth of numerical semigroups of a given genus (Semigroup Forum)

title: Descartes/Soddy: three mutually tangent circles of radii x,y,z have inner Soddy curvature 1/x+1/y+1/z + 2√((x+y+z)/xyz)
connection: ES fixes the linear part to 4/n; rationality of the Soddy curvature additionally needs (x+y+z)/(xyz) to be a rational square. Links ES to Apollonian-type curvature questions (F08 via HKRS).
why: A sub-family of ES solutions inside integral Apollonian configurations would inherit thin-orbit tools.
first_step: Count ES solutions (p ≤ 10⁵) where (x+y+z)·xyz is a square; if non-empty, look for Apollonian structure.

title: Shrinking-target / hitting-time for the Gauss map: λ(p) ≤ 3 as 'some orbit hits a target in ≤ 3 steps'
connection: ES₅: for each p there is q with p/q of continued-fraction length ≤ 3 (with constraints). In dynamics language: some rational point of denominator p reaches a target set within 3 Gauss-map steps.
why: Effective equidistribution of rationals with denominator p under the Gauss map (Ustinov, Bykovskii) could give counts of such q with a main term ≍ log²p.
first_step: Check Ustinov's results on the statistics of continued-fraction lengths of a/p for fixed p (number of a with length ≤ k).
refs: unverified: Ustinov, On the statistical properties of elements of continued fractions (Doklady)

title: Collatz (Tao 2019): almost all orbits attain almost bounded values via logarithmic density — the exceptional-set-improvement analogue
connection: ∀n conjecture (F01), almost-all known (F05), huge verification (F23), heuristic support (F24). Tao's key was changing the measure (logarithmic density) to gain an approximate invariance.
why: ES's exceptional set bound is stuck at exp(−c(log N)^{3/4}) (F40); a change of averaging measure (logarithmic weights in p, or weighting by the BM main term) might likewise gain invariance.
first_step: Recompute the ES exceptional-set argument with logarithmic density in n and see whether the 3/4 barrier changes.

title: ES as a Hurwitz-type equation with a Vieta group: orbit counts per n
connection: Hurwitz equations Σx_i² = a·Πx_i have finitely many fundamental solutions per (n,a) generating trees under Vieta moves; ES's word set has a forest structure (F39). Counting fundamental solutions vs. n is a solved problem type. Caveat: tuv − u − v and the ES cubic are multilinear, so classical Vieta root swaps do not exist on them; the analogue must use other involutions/birational moves.
why: If ES words admit a finite 'fundamental domain' per p, existence reduces to existence of a fundamental solution with bounded size.
first_step: Search for involutions or birational moves on (t,u,v) preserving tuv − u − v = p (e.g. moves through the divisor pairing d ↔ (4Cp+1)/d, swaps across levels) and compute orbit structure for p ≤ 10⁴.
refs: unverified: Hurwitz 1907, Über eine Aufgabe der unbestimmten Analysis

title: Apollonian reciprocity obstructions
connection: Apollonian packings have local congruence conditions and global reciprocity obstructions (F06,F07,F18,F31); ES has a prescribed-entry SL₂ matrix formulation plus congruence constraints (F18).
why: Reciprocity obstructions in a group-orbit setting may reveal hidden global constraints or constructive orbit coverage in ES matrix certificates.
first_step: Read Haag–Kertzer–Rickards–Stange's reciprocity criterion and test whether ES's prescribed-entry matrices admit a comparable spinor/reciprocity invariant.
refs: https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.02749 (Haag–Kertzer–Rickards–Stange, The local-global conjecture for Apollonian circle packings is false; Annals 200 (2024))

title: Generalized Euclidean divisor search for ES certificates
connection: Arxiv:2410.05030 generalizes Lenstra's divisor search to additional Euclidean rings, matching ES F10/F32 and F16's algebraic word encodings.
why: Its algorithmic divisor approach may reveal an efficient search certificate for the particular divisor-in-a-class characterization of ES.
first_step: Check the paper's sequence construction in the ordinary integer case and determine whether the ES tied integer can be fed in without requiring the algorithm's S³>N range.

title: Ordering continuants by local transformations
connection: The operation increasing continuants in arXiv:1608.08322 matches ES F16/F17/F32: bounded continued-fraction words encode integers, and local word changes control their size.
why: A controlled transformation on the ES length-three word may normalize coordinates or push a witness into a useful congruence class.
first_step: Read the operation in the paper and test whether an analogous adjacent-letter move preserves n=tuv−u−v while changing the coordinate residue.

title: Periodic continuant formulas and ES residue periodicity
connection: The explicit periodic-continuant formulas in arXiv:2001.06213 match ES F16/F17/F03, since periodic continued-fraction words can encode structured congruence families.
why: This is a concrete identity toolkit for testing whether periodic ES word patterns generate infinite residue-class families.
first_step: Use the paper's periodic formula on a short periodic word and compare its resulting n-values modulo the ES covering modulus 840.

title: Integral orbit tree versus finite ES residue covers
connection: The Markoff–Hurwitz positive-solution asymptotics in arXiv:2605.05075 match ES F13/F38/F34: an infinite orbit tree is a contrast to ES's need to cover every prime by families.
why: It suggests measuring whether a finite set of ES moves produces enough residue classes or only a thin orbit.
first_step: Compute the mod-840 action of candidate ES coordinate involutions and compare the orbit's residue coverage with the known Mordell covering.

title: Stern continuants and orbit-growth bounds
connection: The explicit transformation/order methods for continuants in arXiv:1608.08322 match ES F16/F17/F38 and the tree-like certificate organization F39.
why: If ES word transformations form a graph, extremal continuant growth could bound the size and depth of its search tree.
first_step: Build the graph of length-three ES word moves induced by continued-fraction identities and test whether the extremal operation from the paper bounds depth at fixed n.

title: A matrix-orbit test for ES certificate connectivity
connection: Markoff matrix/tree encodings in arXiv:0709.1499 match ES F18/F38/F39 and F32: the central question can be reframed as whether short transformations connect all required certificate states.
why: This suggests a finite-state or orbit-connectivity experiment on congruence reductions, directly aligned with the ES word-graph viewpoint.
first_step: Define vertices as ES word certificates modulo a small modulus and test whether candidate matrix generators connect every admissible residue state.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Collatz parity vectors as finite-word certificates
connection: The Collatz problem shares F16w, F22, F32, F23: finite parity words encode trajectories and permit certificate-style computation for a universal integer claim. ES has fixed polynomial/word forms and short certificates (F16,F32).
why: The disciplined separation of word constraints, congruences, and positivity may inspire an ES certificate search with independently checkable proof objects.
first_step: Write a tiny enumerator for ES n=tuv−u−v certificates by bounded word/parameter height and compare its pruning by congruences with Collatz parity-vector pruning.

title: Apollonian curvatures: local-global density one versus every integer
connection: The Apollonian curvature problem shares F03,F05,F10,F23: congruence-allowed values, density-one local-global results, and arithmetic orbit structure. Its known density-one scope contrasts with ES’s pointwise target (F21).
why: The local-global methods combine thin orbits and congruence sieving, a close model for ES where congruence coverage is necessary but not sufficient.
first_step: Read Bourgain–Kontorovich's density-one theorem (arXiv:1205.4416) and isolate its sieve/expansion step; then read the 2024 Annals counterexample paper and ask whether ES's p-tied divisor parametrization can supply an analogous orbit.
refs: https://arxiv.org/abs/1205.4416 (Bourgain–Kontorovich, On the local-global conjecture for integral Apollonian gaskets: density one)

title: Markov triples: mutation trees and orbit enumeration
connection: Markov triples share ES’s integral cubic equation, involutive transformations, thin witness families, and finite checks (F13,F30,F38,F23). Mutation organizes infinitely many solutions from a small seed.
why: A mutation-orbit perspective could reveal whether ES solutions partition into manageable parameter orbits rather than isolated divisor certificates.
first_step: Enumerate low-height ES triples modulo permutation and test for simple rational transformations preserving the defining cubic after fixing n.

title: Three-generator Frobenius numbers as sparse witnesses
connection: The 3-generator Frobenius problem shares F01,F10,F23,F32: arithmetic objects are characterized by integer parameters and modular/divisibility constraints, with finite certificates and computational catalogs. ES similarly searches thin divisor witnesses for each prime.
why: Apéry-set methods convert semigroup membership into finite residue-class data, potentially useful for organizing ES divisors by residue.
first_step: Read a three-generator Frobenius formula and test an Apéry-style residue table for ES’s tied divisor integer 4Cp+1.

title: SL₂(Z) semigroup membership as bounded-word reachability
connection: Matrix-semigroup membership shares F16w,F18,F32,F23: existence asks for a finite word producing a target matrix, with short certificates and decidable bounded searches. ES has a prescribed-entry SL₂ formulation and bounded certificate length.
why: Automata/word-search tools can enumerate structured ES matrix products and exploit congruence states before large integers arise.
first_step: Encode the ES matrix identity as generators and run breadth-first search modulo small moduli, retaining only states compatible with the target entry.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Lüroth expansions and finite digit alphabets
connection: Lüroth and continued-fraction expansions share F17,F18,F32: digits encode rational values by short arithmetic words, with bounded-digit variants producing thin sets. ES also has bounded-length CF/SL₂ descriptions.
why: Alternative expansion algorithms may give a more natural parametrization of positive rational decompositions than continued fractions.
first_step: Search for a Lüroth representation of 4/p with constrained first digits and test whether three digit choices imply an ES decomposition.

title: Zaremba: transfer-operator counting for restricted digits
connection: Restricted-CF denominator problems share F17,F18,F22,F24: thin matrix semigroups are counted via digit words and growth heuristics. ES’s bounded CF length and matrix-entry target invite analogous transfer operators.
why: A transfer operator may estimate how many ES-compatible words exist at a given prime, rather than merely count all integer triples.
first_step: Define a transfer operator for ES’s allowed three-step matrix digits and calculate its predicted count against small-prime data.

title: Apollonian thin-orbit sieve and congruence expansion
connection: Apollonian packings share F03,F05,F10,F22: a thin orbit is sifted among locally allowed integers, yielding density-one coverage. ES’s witness divisors are thin and congruence constrained.
why: The orbit-sieve viewpoint directly addresses why local admissibility may fail to imply a witness for individual primes.
first_step: Read the density-one theorem’s sieve dimension and test whether an ES parameter orbit has comparable equidistribution modulo squarefree moduli.

title: Collatz: density notions and logarithmic sampling
connection: Collatz and ES share F05,F21,F23,F24: strong almost-all/computational evidence leaves pointwise exceptional inputs unresolved. Tao’s logarithmic-density approach makes the quantifier gap explicit.
why: Comparing natural and logarithmic density may tell whether ES exceptional primes are genuinely sparse in the metric relevant to divisor-counting estimates.
first_step: Compute the logarithmic count of ES primes lacking each fixed certificate family over existing bounded data and compare with natural-density counts.

title: Kourovka group problems: SL₂(Z) word reachability
connection: Group word problems share F16w,F18,F32: whether a target element is represented by a word has a short explicit certificate and congruence quotients provide cheap tests. ES has a prescribed-entry SL₂ reachability form.
why: Quotient-group obstructions and normal forms can identify necessary conditions or canonical representatives for ES matrix words.
first_step: Take the ES generator matrices, compute their images in SL₂(Z/mZ) for small m, and compare reachable target-entry states by prime residue.

title: Zaremba and ES: finite alphabet versus finite word length
connection: Both Zaremba and ES use continued fractions and SL₂ words (F17,F18,F32), but Zaremba constrains the digit alphabet while ES constrains word length and matrix entries. This feature flip isolates alphabet complexity from length complexity.
why: Comparing the two constraints may show whether ES can be attacked using a finite alphabet despite variable intermediate parameters.
first_step: Compute partial quotients of the ES₅ representations for small primes and test for a finite digit alphabet covering a positive fraction.

title: Feature flip F39: Stern–Brocot / Calkin–Wilf trees enumerate every rational exactly once — is there a tree enumerating ES words with p at a bounded depth?
connection: Universality of a tree enumeration is trivial for rationals; ES's word forest (F39) has connectivity results. A tree in which every prime appears within bounded depth would prove ES₅-type statements.
why: Gives a combinatorial reformulation: bounded-depth covering in an explicit tree (like λ(p) ≤ 3 in the Euclid tree).
first_step: Compute the depth of each hard prime in the Stern–Brocot-type tree generated by the ES₅ moves; check bounded depth up to 10⁸.

title: Golsefidy–Varjú superstrong approximation for the ES₅ semigroup
connection: Salehi Golsefidy–Varjú prove expansion for perfect groups' congruence quotients; ES₅ words generate a semigroup in SL₂(ℤ) whose Zariski closure and congruence images are computable.
why: Determines whether the ES₅ semigroup has full congruence image mod every q (local-global input).
first_step: Compute the Zariski closure and mod-q images of the semigroup generated by the ES₅ letters for small q.
refs: Salehi Golsefidy–Varjú, Expansion in perfect groups, GAFA 22 (2012)

title: Magee–Oh–Winter uniform congruence counting for Schottky semigroups
connection: MOW give uniform spectral gap/congruence counting for thin Schottky semigroups; underlying tool for Zaremba-type local-global.
why: If ES₅ admits a Schottky-semigroup formulation with unbounded alphabet truncated at height T, uniform counting mod q gives local-global for almost all.
first_step: Check whether truncating ES₅ letters to digits ≤ A yields a Schottky semigroup and compute its Hausdorff dimension δ_A as A grows.
refs: Magee–Oh–Winter, Uniform congruence counting for Schottky semigroups in SL2(Z), Crelle 753 (2019)

title: Bourgain–Fuchs / Bourgain–Kontorovich density-one Apollonian method for ES siblings
connection: Positive-density and density-one results for Apollonian curvatures use thin-orbit circle methods with a quadratic subfamily (shifted binary forms); ES certificates are also quadratic-form values (p² + 4c²d).
why: Transfer of the 'quadratic subfamily + large sieve' trick to ES certificate families.
first_step: Identify a sub-family of ES certificates that is a shifted binary quadratic form in two free parameters at fixed p, and apply the BK almost-all argument.
refs: Bourgain–Kontorovich, On the local-global conjecture for integral Apollonian gaskets, Invent. Math. 196 (2014)

title: Einsiedler–Margulis–(Mohammadi–)Venkatesh effective equidistribution of closed semisimple orbits
connection: EMV/EMMV give effective equidistribution of closed orbits of semisimple groups (e.g. SO(Q) for ternary Q) with polynomial rates; ES has ternary-form and quaternion reformulations.
why: Closed-orbit equidistribution yields local-global for representations of large integers by forms — with effective rates, potentially of a whole genus.
first_step: Pick the repo's ternary/quaternion ES reformulation (QUATERNION_ES.md) and identify the closed orbit whose equidistribution would give the needed representations.
refs: Einsiedler–Margulis–Venkatesh, Effective equidistribution for closed orbits of semisimple groups on homogeneous spaces, Invent. Math. 177 (2009), arXiv:0708.4040
Einsiedler–Margulis–Mohammadi–Venkatesh, Effective equidistribution and property (τ), JAMS 33 (2020), arXiv:1503.05884

title: Duke–Imamoḡlu–Tóth cycle integrals for ES₅ geodesic data
connection: DIT express traces of modular functions over closed geodesics (indefinite forms) as coefficients of mock modular forms; ES₅/CF-length data is geodesic (Hirzebruch–Jung, Dedekind) data of rationals tied to p.
why: A mock-modular generating function for CF-statistics could encode ES₅ counts with exact modular transformation laws.
first_step: Compute the DIT-style generating function Σ_D Tr_D(f) for f = indicator-like modular function and check whether CF length-3 counts appear.
refs: Duke–Imamoḡlu–Tóth, Cycle integrals of the j-function and mock modular forms, Ann. Math. 173 (2011)

title: Geodesic-flow coding (Series) of γ_w: ES₅ as a closed geodesic with 3 cusp excursions of prescribed depths
connection: Caroline Series' coding links the cutting sequence of a geodesic to its CF expansion, so cusp-excursion depths correspond to partial quotients. A word gives a closed geodesic whose (HJ) coding has 3 blocks of depths (v, t, u), plus a p-condition.
why: Shrinking-target and logarithm-law results (Sullivan) describe cusp excursions statistically. Prescribed exact-depth triples relate to 'periodic orbits with prescribed excursions' counts (Pollicott, Lalley).
first_step: Count closed geodesics whose coding is exactly a 3-block HJ word with depths in given ranges; compare with the word count via the p-constraint.
alt_first_steps: [tools-0178] Draw, for hard primes, the Farey path of the relevant rationals and record the minimal crossing count; compare with the length-3 requirement.
refs: Series, The modular surface and continued fractions (J. LMS 1985)
Series, The modular surface and continued fractions, J. LMS 31 (1985)

title: Ramanujan Machine-style search for polynomial-CF identities producing ES₅ words
connection: The Ramanujan Machine (Raayoni et al., Nature 2021) searches polynomial continued fractions for constant identities; ES₅ solutions are short CF words with entries polynomial in parameters (Mordell families).
why: Automated search over polynomial CF word families could find new parametric families covering more residue classes.
first_step: Enumerate length-3 ES₅ words whose entries are degree-≤2 polynomials in t with small coefficients and record which residue classes mod 840·k they cover.
refs: Raayoni et al., Generating conjectures on fundamental constants with the Ramanujan Machine, Nature 590 (2021)

title: OAI 018 Margulis–Platonov (claimed) — normal subgroups of SL₂ over global fields for ES words
connection: OAI 018 claims Margulis–Platonov over number fields; normal-subgroup structure of arithmetic groups matters for congruence-subgroup and thin-group questions about ES₅ words.
why: Very indirect; listed for completeness of the SL₂-word line.
first_step: Close unless an ES SL₂ formulation needs non-congruence normal subgroups.

title: Word-map surjectivity (Larsen–Shalev; Ore conjecture) for ES₅ word shapes
connection: Larsen–Shalev show word maps w: G^k → G are surjective (or nearly) for large finite simple groups; ES₅ is a specific word shape with constrained letters in SL₂.
why: Surjectivity of the ES word map on SL₂(𝔽_q) (with letter constraints) is the local-at-q statement; failures at small q explain local obstructions.
first_step: Define the constrained ES₅ word map over 𝔽_q and compute its image size for q ≤ 100.
refs: Larsen–Shalev, Word maps and Waring type problems, JAMS 22 (2009)

title: Helfgott growth in SL₂(𝔽_p) for the set of ES₅ letters
connection: Helfgott: generating sets A of SL₂(𝔽_p) satisfy |AAA| ≥ |A|^{1+δ} unless A is nearly the group; the ES₅ letter set at p is a specific subset.
why: Growth explains how quickly length-k words cover the group; ES fixes k = 3 so the growth exponent needed is computable.
first_step: Measure |A|, |A²|, |A³| mod small primes for the ES₅ letter set restricted to letters of height ≤ p.
refs: Helfgott, Growth and generation in SL2(Z/pZ), Ann. Math. 167 (2008)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings
